title: The Architecture of Expertise: Maya Notices the Experts Have Stopped Going Home
author: Richard Claydon
summary: Through a fictionalised consulting-firm narrative, Claydon argues that generative AI's real effect on professional services isn't replacing expertise but relocating the bottleneck from production to judgement. As junior staff produce polished, plausible work far faster than before, senior experts absorb an ever-growing volume of verification, exception-handling, and client repair, and the ordinary mid-difficulty work that once let juniors learn judgement alongside a mentor disappears first because it's exactly the work AI performs well. The essay warns that firms measuring only drafting time saved are missing the other side of the ledger — review time, rework, and the vanishing apprenticeship through which professional judgement has always been built — and that a profession's future depends on protecting some of that developmental work even when AI could complete it faster.
points: The productivity gain is real but incomplete: as junior output triples, the partners reviewing that output remain exactly as numerous and no faster at verifying it, so the bottleneck moves from production to judgement.

Plausibility has become cheap: AI lets someone produce a polished market analysis or regulatory summary before they've developed an equivalent depth of understanding, and fluent prose makes that gap harder to see.

The ordinary, moderate-difficulty work that once let juniors learn beside an expert disappears first, because it's exactly the work AI performs well — removing the apprenticeship through which judgement has always formed.

A cheap output can produce an expensive assured outcome: the real productivity question spans the cost of producing credible work, the cost of checking whether it deserves trust, and the cost of repairing it when confidence outruns understanding.

Capacity is a system property, not a point measurement — a true AI productivity metric needs review time, rework, escalation load, and preserved developmental opportunities alongside documents produced and drafting time saved.
quotes: The consultant could explain the recommendation. They could not reconstruct how the evidence justified it.

The cost of producing an apparently credible answer has fallen much faster than the cost of knowing whether the answer deserves to be trusted. That changes the economics of professional work. Production becomes abundant. Judgement becomes scarce.

Much of that ordinary work was exactly where AI performed well. So it disappeared first. What remained for the experts became increasingly concentrated around exceptions, ambiguous evidence, weakly understood recommendations, high-consequence judgement, client repair and urgent escalation.

A junior consultant who can produce partner-quality prose has not necessarily developed partner-quality judgement. The distinction can remain hidden for quite a long time. Their documents look better. Their output increases.
A productivity dashboard counted output. It rarely counted cognitive congestion. It did not show the experienced specialist switching continuously between unrelated high-consequence questions.
